statement: There exists a mixed-sign Coxeter system which does not satisfy the Deletion Property.
proof: Consider the mixed-sign Coxeter graph \widetilde{A}_{-2} in Figure 3.11. The mixed-sign Coxeter group is generated by three generators. W(\widetilde{A}_{-2}) := \langle s_1, s_2, s_3 \rangle. We think of these as the matrices s_1 := [-1, -1, -1; 0, 1, 0; 0, 0, 1], s_2 := [1, 0, 0; -1, -1, -1; 0, 0, 1], s_3 := [1, 0, 0; 0, 1, 0; -1, -1, -1]. By Lemma 3.17 we know that the group must have the relations s_1^2 = s_2^2 = s_3^2 = (s_1 s_2)^3 = (s_2 s_3)^3 = (s_1 s_3)^3 = 1. (3.21.1) Working towards a contradiction, assume that W(\widetilde{A}_{-2}) only has the relations in 3.21.1, a group with only these relations would then have infinite order. Then W(\widetilde{A}_{-2}) has infinite order. A computation of the matrices shows that we also have the relation (s_1 s_2 s_3)^4 = 1. (3.21.2) Again, assuming (W, S, B(\widetilde{A}_{-2})) has the Deletion Property then the relation 3.21.2 must be a consequence of 3.21.1. However, the computer software GAP [GAP08] gives an isomorphism to the permutation group S_4: W(\widetilde{A}_{-2}) \cong S_4 = \langle (1, 2), (1, 3), (1, 4) \rangle via S_4 \rightarrow W(\widetilde{A}_{-2}), (1, 2) \mapsto [-1, -1, -1; 0, 1, 0; 0, 0, 1] = s_1, (1, 3) \mapsto [1, 0, 0; -1, -1, -1; 0, 0, 1] = s_2, (1, 4) \mapsto [1, 0, 0; 0, 1, 0; -1, -1, -1] = s_3. Since S_4 is a finite group and S_4 \cong W(\widetilde{A}_{-2}) therefore we conclude W(\widetilde{A}_{-2}) is finite. This makes it impossible for the relation 3.21.2 to be a consequence of 3.21.1.
notes: tail_after_qed gives alternative argument via relation (3.21.3) and the 21-deletion check; omitted from proof.

statement: Recall in Theorem 1.4 we show that if \Gamma is bipartite then (W, S, B(\Gamma)) is conjugate to (W, S, B(\Gamma_{-})). The previous example indicates that without the bipartite condition this theorem fails in a non-trivial way, the Coxeter graph \widetilde{A}_2 corresponds to an infinite order reflection group whereas we just proved that \widetilde{A}_{-2} has finite order. We extend this example in Section 3.4 to prove Theorem 1.6.

Interestingly, the group S_4 already appears in classic Coxeter theory as the group that arises from the graph in Figure 3.12. The presentation of W(A_3) is W(A_3) = \langle t_1, t_2, t_3 \rangle where t_1 := [-1, 1, 0; 0, 1, 0; 0, 0, 1], t_2 := [1, 0, 0; 1, -1, 1; 0, 0, 1], t_3 := [1, 0, 0; 0, 1, 0; 0, 1, -1]. Again the computational software GAP [GAP08] gives an isomorphism between S_4 and W(A_3) via (1, 2) \mapsto t_1, (2, 3) \mapsto t_2, (3, 4) \mapsto t_3. We now show one family of mixed-sign Coxeter systems which does not satisfy the Deletion Property, proving Theorem 1.2.

The \widetilde{A}_n mixed-sign Coxeter graph is the cycle consisting of n + 1 positive nodes. The \widetilde{A}_{-n} mixed-sign Coxeter graph is the cycle consisting of n + 1 negative nodes. Notice that a graph is not bipartite exactly when the graph contains an even cycle. The mixed-sign Coxeter graph \widetilde{A}_n where n is even is therefore not bipartite. We show that (W, S, B(\widetilde{A}_n)) is not conjugate to (W, S, B(\widetilde{A}_{-n})). Furthermore we justify our claim n = 2, 4, 6 \widetilde{A}_{-(n)} the mixed-sign Coxeter graph associates to a group which is finite and is isomorphic to finite classical Coxeter group W(D_{n+1}). The GAP [GAP08] code for the n = 4 case is in the appendix, see section D. In [Hum90] it is shown for every n that the \widetilde{A}_n associates to a classical Coxeter system; the bilinear forms are positive semi-definite and the associated reflection groups have infinite order. As we indicated in the proof of Lemma 3.21 we are also able to state the following lemma.
notes: Author's garbled sentence 'our claim n = 2, 4, 6 \widetilde{A}_{-(n)} ...' kept verbatim from source.

statement: There exists an odd-cycle mixed-sign Coxeter graph \Gamma with W(\Gamma) not isomorphic to W(\Gamma_{-}).
proof: We apply Lemma 3.17 on the mixed-sign Coxeter graph \widetilde{A}_2 in Figure 3.13. Since the \widetilde{A}_2 graph is a classical Coxeter graph, then we conclude that the group has the presentation W(\widetilde{A}_2) = \langle s_1, s_2, s_3 \mid s_1^2 = s_2^2 = s_3^2 = (s_1 s_2)^3 = (s_2 s_3)^3 = (s_1 s_3)^3 = 1 \rangle. As we indicated in the proof of Lemma 3.21 the group W(\widetilde{A}_2) has infinite order. Whereas, above, we found the group W(\widetilde{A}_{-2}) has finite order.
notes: tail_after_qed announces Theorem 1.6 (non-conjugacy for even n) and generalizes to \widetilde{A}_{-n}.

statement: In Lemma 3.21 we show that (W, S, B(\widetilde{A}_{-2})) does not satisfy the Deletion Property. In doing so, we also show that W(\widetilde{A}_{-2}) is a finite order group whereas W(\widetilde{A}_2) is an infinite order group. We further remark that W(\widetilde{A}_{-n}) when n = 4 and n = 6 also has finite order. Again, we use the computer algebra system GAP [GAP08] to determine that the orders are 1920 and 322560, respectively. This implies that the groups are finite reflection groups. From standard Coxeter theory, the only Coxeter groups with these orders correspond to the D_5 and D_7 classical Coxeter graphs in A.1. Appendix D contains GAP code which shows explicitly shows the isomorphism between W(\widetilde{A}_{-4}) and W(D_5). We conjecture that if n is even then W(\widetilde{A}_n) has finite order and W(\widetilde{A}_{-n}) is isomorphic to W(D_{n+1}) where D_n is the classical Coxeter graph in Table A.1.
notes: Author's typo 'shows explicitly shows' kept verbatim.

statement: Suppose w is a Coxeter element in a classical Coxeter group W then: If w has eigenvalues of modulus 1, and 1 is not an eigenvalue then the Coxeter system is spherical; If w has eigenvalues of modulus 1 and 1 is an eigenvalue then the Coxeter system is affine; If w has eigenvalues which are greater than 1 then the Coxeter system is hyperbolic or higher-rank. Furthermore, the eigenvalue of the graph of a classical Coxeter system is directly related to the spectral radius of Coxeter elements. Let \Gamma_1 and \Gamma_2 be two classical Coxeter graphs. We say that \Gamma_1 \subset \Gamma_2 if there is a map \varphi : \Gamma_1 \rightarrow \Gamma_2 such that \varphi : Nodes(\Gamma_1) \rightarrow Nodes(\Gamma_2) is injective; m(i, j) = m(\varphi(i), \varphi(j)) when \varphi(i) and \varphi(j) are defined.

title: Interlacing Theorem for classical Coxeter graphs
statement: (Interlacing Theorem for classical Coxeter graphs) Suppose \Gamma is a classical Coxeter graph and w_1 is a Coxeter element of W(\Gamma). Suppose r_i \in Node\Gamma and w_2 is a Coxeter element of W(\Gamma/(r_i)) then \lambda(w_1) > \lambda(w_2).
proof: The result follows from the standard interlacing theorem for graphs or positive matrices see [MS05] and [McM02].

statement: Consider the A_3(+, +, -) mixed-sign Coxeter graph in Figure 3.14. The mixed-sign Coxeter graph A_3(+, +, -) has an associated bilinear form B = [2, -1, 0; -1, 2, -1; 0, -1, -2] which has signature (2, 1, 0). Therefore, A_3(+, +, -) is a hyperbolic mixed-sign Coxeter graph. The spectral radius of a principal element in the A_3(+, +, -) system is 1. This indicates that the method of using the spectral radius of a principal element given by [A'C76] in Theorem 3.27, will not extend to the mixed-sign case. Furthermore, recall the A_2(+, -) mixed-sign Coxeter graph in Figure 3.9. Notice that, A_2(+, -) \subset A_3(+, +, -). After some computations we find \chi(A_2(+, -), x) = x^2 + 3x + 1 and \chi(A_3(+, +, -), x) = x^3 + 3x^2 + 3x + 1 and we notice 1 = \Lambda(A_3(+, +, -)) < \Lambda(A_2(+, -)) = (3 + \sqrt{5})/2 \approx 2.618 so Theorem 3.28 also fails to extend to mixed-sign Coxeter systems.

We refer to Table B.1 and Table B.2 notice that we have a sequence of graphs A_2(+, -) \subset A_3(-, +, +) \subset A_4(-, +, +, +) \subset A_5(-, +, +, +, +) whith 2.618 \approx \Lambda(A_2(+, -)) > \Lambda(A_3(-, +, +)) = 1, 1 = \Lambda(A_3(-, +, +)) < \Lambda(A_4(-, +, +, +)) \approx 2.153 and 2.153 \approx \Lambda(A_4(-, +, +, +)) > \Lambda(A_5(-, +, +, +, +)) \approx 1.883. That is, each of the A_n-type graphs above is obtained by adding a positive node to the preceding graph. However, The spectral radius of the graphs is not monotone.
notes: Author's typos 'whith' and 'However, The spectral radius' kept verbatim.

statement: For a bipartite mixed-sign Coxeter graph \Gamma define a bipartite principal element to be a principal element which has the form rg where r = \prod_{i \in N_1} s_{\sigma(i)} and g = \prod_{j \in N_2} s_{\sigma(j)} where N_1 and N_2 are disjoint set of nodes for a bipartite ordering of \Gamma.
notes: Trailing Figure 3.15 and Table 3.1 belong to Example 3.33 and were dropped.

statement: All bipartite principal elements are in the same conjugacy class.
proof: We assume a bipartite ordering on the nodes of \Gamma, let N_1 and N_2 be as in Definition 2.40. If i, j \in N_1 then there are no edges connecting i and j and we have that s_i s_j = s_j s_i, so letters in r may be interchanged. Similarly, letters in g may also be interchanged.
notes: tail_after_qed concludes bipartite elements have equal spectral radius.

statement: Consider the bipartite mixed-sign Coxeter graph in Figure 3.15 and Table 3.1. Table 3.1 gives the Coxeter element corresponding to the node labeling in Figure 3.15, the spectral radius of the Coxeter element, and the “type of Coxeter element”. As the table indicates, the spectral radius of the bipartite principal element is not the smallest spectral radius among other principal elements listed.
notes: Table 3.1 rows dropped; bipartite principal element (s_5 s_2 s_1 s_3)(s_4 s_6) has spectral radius 7.14809.

statement: There exists a bipartite mixed-sign Coxeter graph which has a bipartite principal element whose spectral radius does not minimize spectral radius among other spectral radii of other principal elements in the reflection group.
Is there a “type” of principal element which minimizes the spectral radius among principal elements in a mixed-sign Coxeter system?
